newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu coalition intact after corruption crisis.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu coalition intact after corruption crisis.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu held his government together on Monday after prosecutors decided not to try him for corruption, but opponents launched an uphill fight in court to try to force an indictment.
Legal experts said chances the court would force the prosecution to press charges were slim.
The scandal has sidelined efforts to pull Middle East peace efforts out of deep crisis.

Prosecutors on Sunday rejected a police recommendation that they should charge Netanyahu with fraud and breach of trust in the short-lived appointment in January of Roni Bar-On as attorney-general, allegedly as part of a shady deal with a political ally on trial for corruption.

Netanyahu hoped to satisfy two cabinet ministers who had threatened to quit over the scandal when he announced he was forming a new advisory committee on senior appointments and government procedures.
Netanyahu's spokesman said in a statement that the Israeli leader had decided to set up the committee after consulting Industry and Trade Minister Natan Sharansky and Finance Minister Dan Meridor.
Sharansky, head of the seven-member Yisrael ba-Aliya party, and Meridor, of Netanyahu's own Likud party, both withdrew their threats to bolt after prosecutors released their report.

Israeli opposition lawmakers and a public watchdog group went to the High Court of Justice on Monday demanding Netanyahu be charged, saying the prosecution's decision to close the case for lack of evidence despite "real suspicions" was "highly unreasonable".

Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat called the "Bar-On affair" an internal Israeli matter but warned Netanyahu not to take actions against Palestinians to try to divert attention from his problems at home.

Israeli troops wounded five Palestinians in a clash in the West Bank village of Sourif where the Israeli army wanted to demolish the home of a resident suspected of involvement in killing several Israelis over two years.

Market reaction to the events could not be gauged since the Tel Aviv Stock exchange was closed on Monday and Tuesday for the start of the seven-day Passover holiday. Due to the holiday no political developments were expected before Tuesday night.

"This government lost its moral basis. We believe all personalities concerned should be indicted and this is the reason we are here to appeal to the Supreme Court," said leftist legislator Yossi Sarid, who filed one of three court challenges.
A former justice minister, David Libai of the Labour party, doubted the appeals would succeed.
"I don't think the High Court will overturn the conclusions of the state attorney," Libai told army radio. "The chance the appeals will succeed to force an indictment is very slim."
Netanyahu, 47, said in a televised speech immediately after prosecutors issued their 75-page report: "The bottom line is I didn't commit any crime and the attorney-general confirmed that."
He apologised for any mistakes in the January appointment, but he said the media and opposition had tried to use the affair "to overthrow the government."
A poll of 502 Israelis for Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper after the prosecutor's report found 58 percent did not think Netanyahu had to resign over the affair while 40 percent thought he did.
